h1: Beer with tandoori food and kebabs
title: Beer With Tandoori Food and Kebabs | Craft Beer School
desc: How char, smoke, yoghurt marinades and chilli change the beer you want with tandoori chicken, seekh kebab, malai tikka, paneer and fish.
teaser: Charcoal and roasted malt speak the same language. That is the shortcut to pairing beer with tandoori food.
standfirst: The tandoor gives food char, smoke and a crust that a cooler kitchen cannot copy. We explain which beers meet that char, which ones clash with it and what to pour with each kebab on the platter.
sections: What the tandoor does to food

A tandoor is a clay oven heated with charcoal or wood. It runs at several hundred degrees. Meat goes in on long skewers after a marinade of yoghurt, ginger, garlic, Kashmiri chilli and garam masala. The heat browns the surface fast through the Maillard reaction and blackens the edges. Fat dripping onto the coals sends smoke back up into the meat.

So tandoori food brings browned, savoury flavour, real bitterness from the charred edges, smoke and a tang from the yoghurt. That is a different set of flavours from a curry. It opens up beers that would be wrong with a butter chicken.

One more variable is the side plate. Mint chutney, sliced onion and lime all add freshness and bite, which is why a platter that tastes heavy on its own feels lighter with them. Count them in when you choose the beer.

The closest match to char in a beer is roasted malt. Roasted malts such as chocolate and black malt are taken in a drum roaster to well over 200 °C, the same family of browning reactions that happens on a skewer. A beer brewed with a little of that malt carries toast, cocoa and coffee notes that sit naturally beside charred meat.

That points to darker lagers first. A German dunkel or a schwarzbier has roast flavour without much weight, so it stays refreshing in Indian heat. An American brown ale or an English porter adds more body for a big mixed grill.

There is one catch. Char bitterness and hop bitterness add up. A heavily hopped beer next to blackened chicken can taste harsh and ashy. Our piece on how we perceive bitterness explains why the two stack. Keep the IBU moderate and let the malt do the matching.

Classic tandoori chicken, red with Kashmiri chilli and finished with lime and chaat masala, takes a dunkel or an amber lager well. The caramel and toast in the malt round off the chilli. The lime and raw onion on the side handle the rest.

Seekh kebab, minced lamb or chicken with green chilli, coriander and spices, pressed onto skewers, is fattier and smokier. A brown ale or a robust porter is a good partner. If you like smoke, a German rauchbier, brewed with beechwood-smoked malt, is a bold match. Try a small glass first, since it divides tables.
Malai tikka, reshmi kebab and galouti

The cream-based kebabs are a different job. Malai tikka uses cream, cheese, cardamom and white pepper rather than red chilli. Reshmi kebab is similarly mild and silky. Here roast would overpower the food.

Pour a Munich helles or a Belgian blonde. The helles keeps things clean. The blonde's fruitier yeast picks up the cardamom. Lucknow's galouti kebab, so soft it barely holds together and fragrant with fine spice, also likes a helles or a gently hopped pilsner.
Paneer tikka, tandoori fish and vegetables

Paneer tikka, often grilled with capsicum and onion, has char on the outside and a mild, milky centre. A saison handles both: its dry, peppery finish meets the spice and its high carbonation cuts the paneer. A Vienna lager is a safer option.

Tandoori fish, or Amritsari fish if it comes battered and fried, wants something lighter. A crisp pilsner or a witbier with its coriander and orange peel keeps the fish delicate. Tandoori mushroom and soya chaap behave more like the meat kebabs and are happy with an amber lager.

Most people do not eat one kebab. They order a platter. In that case pick two beers rather than hunting for one that suits everything: something dark and malty for the red and charred items, plus something pale and crisp for the cream kebabs, the fish and the paneer. A dunkel and a pilsner cover nearly any tandoori platter between them.

Then pay attention to what changes as you switch. You may notice that the pilsner tastes more bitter after the chicken, or that the dunkel makes the malai tikka taste flat. Spotting and naming effects like these is the core of sensory training. It is also what separates a guess from a good pairing.
faqs: What beer goes best with tandoori chicken?
A dark lager such as a dunkel or schwarzbier, or an amber lager. Their roasted or toasty malt matches the char while the moderate bitterness avoids a harsh finish.
Do hoppy IPAs go with kebabs?
With caution. Hop bitterness adds to the bitterness of charred edges and to the chilli heat. A moderately hopped pale ale works better than a strong IPA.
What beer goes with paneer tikka?
A saison or a Vienna lager. The saison's carbonation cuts the paneer and its peppery finish suits the spice.
A Munich helles or a Belgian blonde. The cream and cardamom are delicate, so skip roasted or heavily hopped beers.
